lesson.title: Edge Cases: Testing the Inputs Nobody Thinks Of
lesson.summary: An edge case is an unusual but still valid input, empty, single-element, all-negative, or otherwise atypical, and deliberately writing test cases for them catches bugs that never show up when you only test the inputs that feel normal.
lesson.body:
You already know how to write a test case, an input paired with the expected output your code should produce for it. Most of the test cases people write first are what you might call the happy path, ordinary, typical inputs that resemble whatever example first came to mind. Edge cases are the deliberate, disciplined opposite of that instinct: they are inputs that sit at the extreme or unusual end of what a function might legitimately receive, an empty list, a list with exactly one item, all negative numbers, the number zero, duplicate values, the largest or smallest value a type can hold. None of these are invalid, a function that processes lists absolutely might receive an empty one, but they are exactly the inputs that get skipped when you only test with whatever felt natural to type first.

The reason this matters so much is that code frequently works perfectly on typical inputs while quietly breaking on the atypical ones, because the logic was written with the typical case in mind and the edge case was never actually pictured while writing it. Deliberately asking yourself, before you consider a function finished, what is the smallest input this could receive, what happens if the input is empty, what if every value is identical, is often the single fastest way to find real bugs.

```python
def find_max(numbers):
    if not numbers:
        return None
    biggest = numbers[0]
    for n in numbers[1:]:
        if n > biggest:
            biggest = n
    return biggest

print(find_max([3, 7, 2, 9, 4]))
print(find_max([5]))
print(find_max([]))
print(find_max([-3, -1, -7]))
```

The first call is the happy path, an ordinary list of several distinct positive numbers, and it correctly walks through 3, 7, 2, 9, 4, updating biggest whenever a larger value shows up, ending at 9. The remaining three calls are all edge cases. find_max([5]) is a single-element list, the for loop over numbers[1:] never executes at all since there is nothing after the first element, so the function correctly falls through to returning numbers[0], which is 5. find_max([]) is the empty-list edge case, where not numbers is True for an empty list, so the function returns None immediately rather than crashing when it tries to access numbers[0] on a list with no elements. find_max([-3, -1, -7]) is the all-negative-numbers edge case, biggest correctly starts at numbers[0], which is -3, not at 0, so it still finds -1 as the largest value. The output is:

```
9
5
None
-1
```

That last case is worth sitting with, because it shows exactly why edge cases catch real bugs. A tempting but subtly wrong version of this function might initialize biggest = 0 instead of biggest = numbers[0], reasoning that 0 is a safe starting point. That version would pass the first two calls without any problem, but it would silently return 0 for find_max([-3, -1, -7]), a wrong answer, since 0 is not even in the list, and every real value is smaller than it. Only a test case built specifically to probe the all-negative edge would ever catch that bug, testing only positive numbers, the case that feels normal, would let it ship.
